206	
207	## 7. BUGS AND HAZARDS IN THE EXISTING FIRMWARE (fix before first power-on)
208	
209	1. **`BTN_6_PIN = 12` will prevent the board from booting.** GPIO 12 (MTDI) is sampled at reset to select flash voltage. `INPUT_PULLUP` holds it high, which selects 1.8 V and bricks the boot. **Move button 6 to GPIO 13.**
210	
211	2. **HC-SR04 ECHO outputs 5 V into a 3.3 V pin.** The ESP32 is not 5 V tolerant. Add a divider on ECHO: 1 kΩ from ECHO to the GPIO, 2 kΩ from the GPIO to GND. (Alternative: buy an RCWL-1601 / HC-SR04+, which is 3.3 V safe. Buy one while in Sétif as a backup.) Note that HC-SR04 still needs **5 V on VCC** to work reliably.
212	
213	3. **`pulseIn` timeout of 60 ms blocks the whole loop.** The robot claims 20 Hz telemetry (50 ms budget) but a missing echo stalls for 60 ms, so the watchdog timing and telemetry rate become unreliable. Reduce the timeout to **25 ms** (≈4.3 m, beyond the sensor's useful range anyway) and only ping every 100 ms rather than every loop.
214	
215	4. **RSSI is a hard-coded placeholder (−50 dBm).** It displays a fabricated number as measured telemetry. In a defense this is a serious credibility problem if noticed. Either extract real RSSI, or replace it with **packet loss % and link latency**, computed from a sequence counter in the packet. Packet loss is a better link-quality metric anyway and is trivial to compute.
216	
217	5. **I2C is at the default 100 kHz.** A full 128×64 frame is 1024 bytes ≈ 100 ms at 100 kHz, which saturates the claimed 10 Hz display rate and blocks everything else. Add `Wire.setClock(400000);` in setup.
218	
219	6. **`BATTERY_DIVIDER` is 2 on the controller and 3 on the robot**, both placeholders. Measure the actual resistors and verify against a multimeter. Also note the ESP32 ADC is non-linear near the rails; keep the divided voltage between roughly 0.3 V and 2.8 V.
220	
221	7. **GPIO 5 as motor PWM** is a strapping pin that must be high at boot; some boards output a PWM pulse on it during boot. With a motor driver attached this can cause a brief unexpected motor twitch on power-up. Moved to GPIO 19 in the map above.
222	
223	8. **The controller computes `motor_left` / `motor_right` and sends those.** This works, but it means the robot cannot change its own mixing or apply obstacle-avoidance overrides cleanly. Consider sending `x`, `y` and letting the robot mix. **Low priority — only if time allows.** Do not refactor this in week 5.
224	
225	---
226	
227	## 8. THE SHARED PROTOCOL HEADER (highest-value software decision)
228	
229	Because the two of you will be **geographically separated during integration**, the link between the two firmwares must be frozen in a single shared file, committed to git, that both projects `#include`. Once this exists, each of you can develop independently against a stub of the other side.
230	
231	Create `include/blocbot_protocol.h`, identical in both PlatformIO projects:
232	
233	```cpp
234	#pragma once
235	#include <stdint.h>
236	
237	#define BLOCBOT_PROTO_VERSION 1
238	
239	enum : uint8_t { MSG_DRIVE = 1, MSG_TELEMETRY = 2 };
240	
241	typedef struct __attribute__((packed)) {
242	  uint8_t  version;      // BLOCBOT_PROTO_VERSION
243	  uint8_t  type;         // MSG_DRIVE
244	  uint16_t seq;          // increments every packet, wraps
245	  int16_t  motor_left;   // -255..+255
246	  int16_t  motor_right;  // -255..+255
247	  uint8_t  mode;         // 0 = Learner, 1 = Researcher
248	  uint8_t  buttons;      // bitfield, b0..b5
249	  uint8_t  estop;        // 1 = stop immediately
250	  uint8_t  reserved;
251	} DriveCmd;              // 12 bytes
252	
253	typedef struct __attribute__((packed)) {
254	  uint8_t  version;
255	  uint8_t  type;         // MSG_TELEMETRY
256	  uint16_t seq;          // echoes the last DriveCmd.seq received
257	  int16_t  motor_left;   // actually applied
258	  int16_t  motor_right;
259	  uint16_t battery_mv;
260	  uint16_t distance_cm;  // 0xFFFF = invalid / no echo
261	  int8_t   rssi;         // real value, or omit this field
262	  uint8_t  flags;        // b0 paired, b1 watchdog tripped, b2 obstacle, b3 low batt
263	  uint16_t uptime_s;
264	} Telemetry;             // 18 bytes
265	```
266	
267	The `seq` field is what makes real link telemetry possible: the controller knows how many commands it sent and how many were echoed back, so **packet loss %** and **round-trip latency in ms** both fall out for free. That is a far stronger thing to show a jury than a fake RSSI number.
268	
269	### Stub firmwares (build these in week 1)
270	- `stub_robot.ino` — receives `DriveCmd`, prints it, replies with plausible `Telemetry` (fake battery ramp, fake distance sweep). Lets the **user** develop and demo the full controller UI alone, from home, with no robot.
271	- `stub_controller.ino` — sends a scripted `DriveCmd` sequence. Lets the **friend** test motors and the watchdog with no controller.
272	
273	Once these exist, the 2-week separation stops being a project risk.
274

363	## 11. TESTING
364	
365	### 11.1 Print test coupon (before the full plate)
366	Print a **60 × 60 mm** square of the Waffle Plate at the real thickness, containing at least two of each hole size. This costs ~15 minutes of print time and saves a failed 6-hour print.
367	
368	Measure with calipers:
369	- Actual vs nominal hole diameters. FDM holes print **undersized by roughly 0.1–0.3 mm** because of extrusion overlap. If the 3.2 mm hole measures 3.0 mm, an M3 screw will not pass. Compensate in CAD, don't drill.
370	- Elephant's foot on the first layer shrinks bottom-of-hole diameters further.
371	- Flatness and warping.
372	
373	**Fillet note:** the 0.75 mm fillet works on the *top* edge of a hole. On the *bottom* edge, resting on the build plate, a fillet becomes an unsupported overhang and prints badly. Use a **45° chamfer** on the bottom edge instead of a fillet. This is also probably the real cause of the Fusion 360 fillet error recorded earlier: an over-large radius on geometry too thin to support it.
374	
375	### 11.2 Formal test sequence
376	For every test, record: **objective / setup / procedure / expected / actual / pass-fail / cause if failed / action**. Fill this in as you go and paste it into the report.
377	
378	| # | Test | Pass criterion |
379	|---|---|---|
380	| T01 | Joystick raw range | X and Y sweep full 0–4095, centre stable within ±20 |
381	| T02 | Centre calibration | Calibrated output = 0 ± deadzone when untouched, for 60 s |
382	| T03 | Circular limit | Full diagonal deflection produces magnitude = radius, not radius × √2 |
383	| T04 | Button matrix | All 6 register, no ghosting, no bounce over 100 presses |
384	| T05 | HC-SR04 accuracy | Measured vs tape measure at 10/25/50/100/200 cm, error < 5 % |
385	| T06 | HC-SR04 out of range | Returns invalid, does not return 0 cm or stall the loop |
386	| T07 | ESP-NOW link | 1000 packets sent, loss < 1 % at 1 m |
387	| T08 | ESP-NOW range | Loss vs distance at 1/5/10/20/30 m, indoors and outdoors |
388	| T09 | Latency | Round-trip from seq echo, median and worst case |
389	| T10 | Safety watchdog | Power off the controller mid-drive; motors stop within 500 ms |
390	| T11 | Battery telemetry | Reported mV within 3 % of multimeter across the discharge range |
391	| T12 | Motor stall current | Measured with wheels blocked; below the driver's continuous rating |
392	| T13 | Drive straightness | Robot tracks straight over 3 m with equal commands, or deviation is documented |
393	| T14 | Runtime | Continuous driving until low-battery cutoff, minutes recorded |
394	| T15 | Waffle Plate fit | M3/M4 hardware passes all holes without forcing |
395	| T16 | Module swap | A block is removed and re-mounted in a different position in under 60 s |
396

403	| Risk | Impact | Mitigation |

405	| **Report deadline is earlier than 21 Oct** | Loses 1–3 weeks | Confirm with supervisor on day 1 |
406	| **You and the friend are apart during integration** | Highest structural risk | Shared protocol header + stub firmwares (§8). Plan a physical integration meeting in week 4 **now**, and book travel. |

409	| Live demo fails during defense | Catastrophic on the day | Pre-recorded demo video + pre-flashed spare boards |
410	| Motor stall current exceeds the driver | Driver dies mid-project | Measure in week 1, buy two driver types |
411	| Scope creep (Smart Blocks, ROS, camera, app) | Runs out the clock | **Feature freeze 7 October.** Anything not started by then becomes "Future Work" in the report, which is a legitimate chapter. |
412	| 5-month knowledge gap | Slow restart | Re-run the test firmware first. Reading your own working code is the fastest way to remember. |

414	**On scope:** it is far better to defend a modest robot that provably works, with a complete test log and honest documentation, than an ambitious one that doesn't. Every unfinished feature you cut becomes a "Future Work" bullet, and juries reward a clear-eyed roadmap.

418	## 13. LIKELY DEFENSE QUESTIONS — prepare answers now
419	
420	1. Why ESP-NOW instead of WiFi, Bluetooth or LoRa? (Answer: connectionless, ~1–2 ms latency, no AP needed, 250-byte payload is sufficient, peer-to-peer. Have measured latency numbers ready.)
421	2. What happens if the wireless link drops mid-drive? (Answer: 500 ms watchdog, motors stop. **Demonstrate it live.**)
422	3. Why did you deviate from the 3S/4S battery in the proposal? (Answer: motor voltage rating drove the change. Show the calculation.)
423	4. Why PETG and not PLA or ABS? (Impact resistance, layer adhesion, less brittle than PLA, easier than ABS, no enclosure needed.)
424	5. Why three hole sizes? (M3 clearance = 3.2 mm, M4 clearance = 4.5 mm, 6.0 mm for standoffs and cable routing. Say exactly this.)
425	6. What is your grid pitch and why? (You must decide and be able to justify it. A 10 mm pitch is clean, metric and compatible with M3/M4 hardware.)
426	7. How does another person build a compatible module? (Point at the published repo and the dimensioned drawing. This is where the open-source objective gets its marks.)
427	8. What is the measured range and packet loss? (Have the T08 table ready.)
428	9. What would you do differently with more time? (Encoders and closed-loop speed control, IMU, PCB instead of jumper wires, more sensor blocks.)
429	10. Which parts are your own work and which are libraries? (Be honest and specific. This question is asked more often than students expect.)

449	- Don't paste a 900-line file and say "fix it". Say what's broken.

**Also:** migrate display code from Adafruit_SSD1306 to **U8g2** now. It supports SSD1306, SH1106, SSD1309 and more behind one API, which makes the screen upgrade a one-line change instead of a rewrite.

### 5.2 Motors — buy geared motors and delete the gear-reduction problem

The old record spends effort on pulley reduction, printed gears and friction wheels. **Do not build a custom reduction.** Buy motors with a gearbox already attached. This removes an entire mechanical sub-project.

| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| "Yellow" TT gearmotor, 1:48, 3–6 V | Ubiquitous, cheap, comes with matching wheels. ~150 mA free-run, ~1 A stall at 6 V. Perfect for human-pace. Sloppy plastic gearbox, no encoder. |
| N20 metal gearmotor, 6 V or 12 V, ~100–300 RPM | Small, much better quality, optional encoder version. Needs mounting brackets. |

**Recommendation:** buy **4 × TT gearmotors + 4 wheels** (2 spare) as the guaranteed-working baseline, and **2 × N20 with encoders** if available and affordable, as an upgrade path. Buy a caster ball for the third contact point.

### 5.3 Motor driver — decide by measurement, buy by availability

The rule from the existing record still holds: measure stall current before committing. But the practical answer is to buy more than one, because you cannot come back.

| Driver | Max continuous | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| L298N module | ~2 A/ch | Universally available in Algeria. Inefficient, drops ~1.8–2 V, gets hot, needs heatsink. Works fine with TT motors. |
| DRV8833 module | ~1.5 A/ch | Efficient, low voltage drop, 2.7–10.8 V. Best match for TT motors on 2S. |
| TB6612FNG module | ~1.2 A/ch | The sweet spot. Efficient, small, robust. |

**Recommendation:** buy **L298N (guaranteed) + DRV8833 or TB6612FNG (preferred)**. All three are pin-compatible with the existing robot firmware's IN1/IN2 + PWM logic.

### 5.4 Battery — simplify to 2S, and justify the deviation in the report

The 3S/4S concept in the original proposal was written before motor selection. If the motors are 6 V TT gearmotors, 3S/4S is wrong.

**Proposed architecture:**
```
2 × 18650 in series (2S, 7.4 V nominal, 8.4 V full)
  → 2S BMS protection board
  → motor driver (motors see ~5.6-6.5V through an L298N, or ~7V through a DRV8833)
  → MP1584 or LM2596 buck converter → 5 V → ESP32 VIN
  → voltage divider → GPIO 36 for battery telemetry
```
This is simpler, safer, cheaper and easier to defend than 4S. **Document the change and the reason** — a deliberate, justified deviation from the proposal reads as engineering maturity in a defense. An unexplained one reads as drift.

Buy: 4 × 18650 cells, 2 × 2S BMS, 2 × buck converters, 1 × 18650 charger, 1 × 2S battery holder. Plus a **multimeter** if you don't own one — non-negotiable.

## 6. PROPOSED PIN MAP (v1 — freeze after validation)

### Critical ESP32 rules that constrain this
1. **ADC2 pins (GPIO 0, 2, 4, 12–15, 25–27) do not work while WiFi/ESP-NOW is active.** All analog inputs must be on **ADC1: GPIO 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 39.** The existing code already gets this right.

## 7. BUGS AND HAZARDS IN THE EXISTING FIRMWARE (fix before first power-on)

1. **`BTN_6_PIN = 12` will prevent the board from booting.** GPIO 12 (MTDI) is sampled at reset to select flash voltage. `INPUT_PULLUP` holds it high, which selects 1.8 V and bricks the boot. **Move button 6 to GPIO 13.**

2. **HC-SR04 ECHO outputs 5 V into a 3.3 V pin.** The ESP32 is not 5 V tolerant. Add a divider on ECHO: 1 kΩ from ECHO to the GPIO, 2 kΩ from the GPIO to GND. (Alternative: buy an RCWL-1601 / HC-SR04+, which is 3.3 V safe. Buy one while in Sétif as a backup.) Note that HC-SR04 still needs **5 V on VCC** to work reliably.

3. **`pulseIn` timeout of 60 ms blocks the whole loop.** The robot claims 20 Hz telemetry (50 ms budget) but a missing echo stalls for 60 ms, so the watchdog timing and telemetry rate become unreliable. Reduce the timeout to **25 ms** (≈4.3 m, beyond the sensor's useful range anyway) and only ping every 100 ms rather than every loop.

4. **RSSI is a hard-coded placeholder (−50 dBm).** It displays a fabricated number as measured telemetry. In a defense this is a serious credibility problem if noticed. Either extract real RSSI, or replace it with **packet loss % and link latency**, computed from a sequence counter in the packet. Packet loss is a better link-quality metric anyway and is trivial to compute.

5. **I2C is at the default 100 kHz.** A full 128×64 frame is 1024 bytes ≈ 100 ms at 100 kHz, which saturates the claimed 10 Hz display rate and blocks everything else. Add `Wire.setClock(400000);` in setup.

6. **`BATTERY_DIVIDER` is 2 on the controller and 3 on the robot**, both placeholders. Measure the actual resistors and verify against a multimeter. Also note the ESP32 ADC is non-linear near the rails; keep the divided voltage between roughly 0.3 V and 2.8 V.

7. **GPIO 5 as motor PWM** is a strapping pin that must be high at boot; some boards output a PWM pulse on it during boot. With a motor driver attached this can cause a brief unexpected motor twitch on power-up. Moved to GPIO 19 in the map above.

8. **The controller computes `motor_left` / `motor_right` and sends those.** This works, but it means the robot cannot change its own mixing or apply obstacle-avoidance overrides cleanly. Consider sending `x`, `y` and letting the robot mix. **Low priority — only if time allows.** Do not refactor this in week 5.

## 8. THE SHARED PROTOCOL HEADER (highest-value software decision)

Because the two of you will be **geographically separated during integration**, the link between the two firmwares must be frozen in a single shared file, committed to git, that both projects `#include`. Once this exists, each of you can develop independently against a stub of the other side.

Create `include/blocbot_protocol.h`, identical in both PlatformIO projects:

```cpp
#pragma once
#include <stdint.h>

#define BLOCBOT_PROTO_VERSION 1

enum : uint8_t { MSG_DRIVE = 1, MSG_TELEMETRY = 2 };

typedef struct __attribute__((packed)) {
  uint8_t  version;      // BLOCBOT_PROTO_VERSION
  uint8_t  type;         // MSG_DRIVE
  uint16_t seq;          // increments every packet, wraps
  int16_t  motor_left;   // -255..+255
  int16_t  motor_right;  // -255..+255
  uint8_t  mode;         // 0 = Learner, 1 = Researcher
  uint8_t  buttons;      // bitfield, b0..b5
  uint8_t  estop;        // 1 = stop immediately
  uint8_t  reserved;
} DriveCmd;              // 12 bytes

typedef struct __attribute__((packed)) {
  uint8_t  version;
  uint8_t  type;         // MSG_TELEMETRY
  uint16_t seq;          // echoes the last DriveCmd.seq received
  int16_t  motor_left;   // actually applied
  int16_t  motor_right;
  uint16_t battery_mv;
  uint16_t distance_cm;  // 0xFFFF = invalid / no echo
  int8_t   rssi;         // real value, or omit this field
  uint8_t  flags;        // b0 paired, b1 watchdog tripped, b2 obstacle, b3 low batt
  uint16_t uptime_s;
} Telemetry;             // 18 bytes
```

The `seq` field is what makes real link telemetry possible: the controller knows how many commands it sent and how many were echoed back, so **packet loss %** and **round-trip latency in ms** both fall out for free. That is a far stronger thing to show a jury than a fake RSSI number.

### Stub firmwares (build these in week 1)
- `stub_robot.ino` — receives `DriveCmd`, prints it, replies with plausible `Telemetry` (fake battery ramp, fake distance sweep). Lets the **user** develop and demo the full controller UI alone, from home, with no robot.
- `stub_controller.ino` — sends a scripted `DriveCmd` sequence. Lets the **friend** test motors and the watchdog with no controller.

Once these exist, the 2-week separation stops being a project risk.

## 11. TESTING

### 11.1 Print test coupon (before the full plate)
Print a **60 × 60 mm** square of the Waffle Plate at the real thickness, containing at least two of each hole size. This costs ~15 minutes of print time and saves a failed 6-hour print.

Measure with calipers:
- Actual vs nominal hole diameters. FDM holes print **undersized by roughly 0.1–0.3 mm** because of extrusion overlap. If the 3.2 mm hole measures 3.0 mm, an M3 screw will not pass. Compensate in CAD, don't drill.
- Elephant's foot on the first layer shrinks bottom-of-hole diameters further.
- Flatness and warping.

**Fillet note:** the 0.75 mm fillet works on the *top* edge of a hole. On the *bottom* edge, resting on the build plate, a fillet becomes an unsupported overhang and prints badly. Use a **45° chamfer** on the bottom edge instead of a fillet. This is also probably the real cause of the Fusion 360 fillet error recorded earlier: an over-large radius on geometry too thin to support it.

### 11.2 Formal test sequence
For every test, record: **objective / setup / procedure / expected / actual / pass-fail / cause if failed / action**. Fill this in as you go and paste it into the report.

| # | Test | Pass criterion |
|---|---|---|
| T01 | Joystick raw range | X and Y sweep full 0–4095, centre stable within ±20 |
| T02 | Centre calibration | Calibrated output = 0 ± deadzone when untouched, for 60 s |
| T03 | Circular limit | Full diagonal deflection produces magnitude = radius, not radius × √2 |
| T04 | Button matrix | All 6 register, no ghosting, no bounce over 100 presses |
| T05 | HC-SR04 accuracy | Measured vs tape measure at 10/25/50/100/200 cm, error < 5 % |
| T06 | HC-SR04 out of range | Returns invalid, does not return 0 cm or stall the loop |
| T07 | ESP-NOW link | 1000 packets sent, loss < 1 % at 1 m |
| T08 | ESP-NOW range | Loss vs distance at 1/5/10/20/30 m, indoors and outdoors |
| T09 | Latency | Round-trip from seq echo, median and worst case |
| T10 | Safety watchdog | Power off the controller mid-drive; motors stop within 500 ms |
| T11 | Battery telemetry | Reported mV within 3 % of multimeter across the discharge range |
| T12 | Motor stall current | Measured with wheels blocked; below the driver's continuous rating |
| T13 | Drive straightness | Robot tracks straight over 3 m with equal commands, or deviation is documented |
| T14 | Runtime | Continuous driving until low-battery cutoff, minutes recorded |
| T15 | Waffle Plate fit | M3/M4 hardware passes all holes without forcing |
| T16 | Module swap | A block is removed and re-mounted in a different position in under 60 s |

T07, T08, T09 and T10 are the ones that make this an *embedded systems* project rather than a toy. Prioritise them.

## 13. LIKELY DEFENSE QUESTIONS — prepare answers now

1. Why ESP-NOW instead of WiFi, Bluetooth or LoRa? (Answer: connectionless, ~1–2 ms latency, no AP needed, 250-byte payload is sufficient, peer-to-peer. Have measured latency numbers ready.)
2. What happens if the wireless link drops mid-drive? (Answer: 500 ms watchdog, motors stop. **Demonstrate it live.**)
3. Why did you deviate from the 3S/4S battery in the proposal? (Answer: motor voltage rating drove the change. Show the calculation.)
4. Why PETG and not PLA or ABS? (Impact resistance, layer adhesion, less brittle than PLA, easier than ABS, no enclosure needed.)
5. Why three hole sizes? (M3 clearance = 3.2 mm, M4 clearance = 4.5 mm, 6.0 mm for standoffs and cable routing. Say exactly this.)
6. What is your grid pitch and why? (You must decide and be able to justify it. A 10 mm pitch is clean, metric and compatible with M3/M4 hardware.)
7. How does another person build a compatible module? (Point at the published repo and the dimensioned drawing. This is where the open-source objective gets its marks.)
8. What is the measured range and packet loss? (Have the T08 table ready.)
9. What would you do differently with more time? (Encoders and closed-loop speed control, IMU, PCB instead of jumper wires, more sensor blocks.)
10. Which parts are your own work and which are libraries? (Be honest and specific. This question is asked more often than students expect.)

STL generation/inspection). Treat FINAL as locked, PROPOSED as needing confirmation before
committing print time, and OPEN as undecided — don't invent a value for it.

## Plate

| Parameter | Value | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Material | PETG | FINAL |
| Large hole diameter | 6.0 mm | FINAL |
| Medium hole diameter | 4.5 mm | FINAL |
| Small hole diameter | 3.2 mm | FINAL |
| Large-hole fillet (top edge) | 0.75 mm | FINAL |
| Bottom-edge treatment | 45° chamfer, not a fillet (fillets on the unsupported bottom edge print as a bad overhang) | FINAL |
| Medium/small hole fillets | — | OPEN |
| Grid pitch | 10 mm proposed | PROPOSED — freeze before generating the full hole pattern |
| Plate outer size | 150–180 mm square | PROPOSED — driven by ~4h print time budget, not final dims |
| Plate thickness | — | OPEN |
| Number of plates | 2, stacked | FINAL |
| Plate spacing | M3 standoffs, 30–50 mm | PROPOSED |
| Print compensation | FDM holes print 0.1–0.3 mm undersized (elephant's foot worsens the bottom layer further) — oversize holes in CAD by this much, don't rely on nominal | FINAL (empirical rule, not measured on this plate yet) |

Lower plate carries motors (mounted via printed brackets using the SAME block footprint below —
not a bespoke mount), driver, battery, robot ESP32. Upper plate carries Smart Blocks only.

## Smart Block mounting — mechanical

**Decided approach:** blocks sit flat on the plate surface and bolt through the existing grid.
No peg-into-hole gripping — FDM hole tolerance is too loose and inconsistent to grip on reliably.

- One **universal 2-hole footprint** for every block type (sensor blocks AND motor brackets).
  Both holes are M3 clearance (3.2 mm), spaced at exactly the grid pitch so the footprint always
  lands on two adjacent grid holes.
- "8 directions" = 8 mounting **locations** spread around the plate perimeter (front, front-right,
  right, back-right, back, back-left, left, front-left) — NOT a rotating single block. This comes
  free from a full perimeter grid at the chosen pitch; no rotate/lock or pivot+slot mechanism needed.
- **OPEN — needs a decision in this session:** does a block need directional keying so a
  direction-sensitive sensor (e.g. HC-SR04, which must face outward to measure correctly) can't be
  bolted on backwards? Options to evaluate: asymmetric footprint (holes not mirror-symmetric),
  one clearance hole + one keyed/offset hole, or a small locating notch against a plate edge/rib.
  Pick whichever is simplest to print reliably at this scale — don't add mechanism for its own sake.
- Footprint should be small enough that adjacent perimeter positions don't foul each other at the
  chosen grid pitch — check this when the pitch is set.

## Electrical connector (for reference only, not a CAD constraint unless keying depends on it)

4-pin standard per block: 5V, GND, SDA/SIG1, SCL/SIG2. I2C blocks (MPU6050 etc.) use SDA/SCL;
simple blocks (HC-SR04 etc.) use the two signal pins as digital I/O.

## What I need from this session

1. Finalize grid pitch (10 mm proposed) and plate outer dimensions within the 150–180 mm target.
2. Design the universal block footprint: exact hole spacing, footprint outer size, and resolve the

4. Once I have an STL, parse it (trimesh / numpy-stl) and report actual bounding box, hole

Final plate thickness, final medium/small fillet radii, final plate outer dimensions (only the
150–180 mm target range is set), final standoff count/positions, final footprint dimensions —
these are exactly what this session is for. Propose values and label them, don't assume them

I used your project files ([BLOC-BOT_Context_and_Plan_v1.md](claude resources/BLOC-BOT_Context_and_Plan_v1.md) and [waffle-plate-smart-block-spec.md](claude resources/waffle-plate-smart-block-spec.md)). Plate thickness and final size aren't decided yet, so the weight below is an estimate. It needs to be checked on a kitchen scale once the robot is built.

## 1. Estimated weight (PROPOSED)

| Part | Assumption | Mass |
|---|---|---|
| 2 × Waffle Plates (PETG) | about 170×170 mm, 3–4 mm thick, perforated, about 40% infill | 120–200 g |
| 4 × Smart Blocks (printed housings) | about 10–15 g each | 40–60 g |
| 4 × sensors | HC-SR04 about 9 g, MPU6050 about 3 g, mixed | 20–40 g |
| 4 × TT gearmotors | about 30 g each | 120 g |
| 4 × wheels (65 mm) | about 25 g each | 100 g |
| 4 × printed motor brackets | about 5 g each | 20 g |
| Motor driver(s) | L298N about 30 g each, DRV8833/TB6612 about 5 g | 10–60 g |
| 2 × 18650 cells + holder + BMS | 47 g per cell | about 115 g |
| ESP32 + buck converter + switch | | about 25 g |
| Standoffs, screws, nuts | M3 | about 40 g |
| Wiring, connectors, zip ties | | about 40 g |
| **Total** | | **about 650–850 g** |

**Size the motors for 1.0 kg.** That leaves room for heavier prints, extra wiring and future blocks.

## 2. Motor sizing (PROPOSED)

Having 4 motors changes the design. The robot becomes **4WD skid-steer**, so you no longer need the caster ball. Skid-steer needs much more torque when turning than when driving straight, because the wheels slide sideways.

**Torque per motor (1 kg robot, 65 mm wheels, radius 0.0325 m):**
- Driving straight (rolling resistance plus acceleration of 0.5 m/s²): about 1 N in total, so about 0.25 N per motor, which is about **0.1 kg·cm**.
- Skid-steer turn on the spot (sideways friction μ ≈ 0.6): about 5.9 N in total, so about 1.5 N per motor, which is about **0.5 kg·cm**.
- With a ×2–3 safety factor, you want **a stall torque of at least 1.0–1.5 kg·cm per motor**.

**Speed:** at a walking pace of about 0.7 m/s with 65 mm wheels, you need 0.7 / (π × 0.065) × 60 ≈ **200 RPM**.

### What to buy
| Spec | Value |
|---|---|
| Type | Geared DC motor (TT 1:48 or N20 metal gearbox) |
| **Rated voltage** | **6 V** |
| Speed | about 150–250 RPM at 6 V |
| Stall torque | at least 1.0 kg·cm (1.5 or more is better) |
| **Running current** | **about 0.2–0.4 A per motor** |
| **Stall current** | **at most 1.5 A per motor** (check the listing) |

Standard TT 1:48 motors meet this, just barely, which matches the many 4WD TT kits of this weight that work fine. If you can find N20 metal-gear motors at 6 V and about 200 RPM, they have more torque margin.

## 3. Whole-system power (PROPOSED)

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Battery | 2S 18650: 7.4 V nominal, 8.4 V full (as planned in §5.4) |
| Normal driving current | 4 × 0.3 A ≈ **1.2–1.5 A** |
| Worst case (all 4 stalled, or a hard turn) | 4 × 1.5 A ≈ **5–6 A** |
| Cells | Rated for **5 A continuous or more** each (Samsung, LG, Sony/Murata). Cheap "9900 mAh" cells can't supply this. |
| BMS | 2S, **8 A or more** continuous |

**Voltage at the motors:**
- **L298N:** it drops about 2 V, so the motors get about 6 V. That's exactly right.
- **DRV8833 or TB6612:** they barely drop any voltage, so the motors get 7.4–8.4 V. That's more than a 6 V motor is rated for, so cap the PWM at about 75% in firmware.

## 4. Driver problem you need to fix

The firmware has only one left and one right channel. With 4 motors, each channel would drive **2 motors in parallel**, which is **up to 3 A per channel** at stall:
- L298N (2 A/channel): overloaded at stall
- DRV8833 (1.5 A) and TB6612 (1.2 A): too small

**Fix: use 2 dual drivers, one channel per motor** (for example 2 × TB6612, 2 × DRV8833 or 2 × L298N). You don't need to change the firmware logic. Wire both left-side channels to the same PWM/IN1/IN2 GPIOs (19/25/26), and do the same for the right side. One ESP32 pin can drive several driver inputs.

## NEEDS TESTING
- **T12:** measure the real stall current with a multimeter and the wheel held still. If it's above 1.5 A, the driver and battery numbers above need to be redone.
- Weigh the finished robot and redo section 2 if it comes out above 1 kg.
- Test a turn on the spot on the actual demo floor surface. Skid-steer on carpet or rubber is the worst case.

Updated. At 80–100% infill, a plate this thin is basically solid PETG.

## Plate mass (PROPOSED, thickness still undecided)

Assumptions: 170×170 mm plate, 10 mm grid with about 16% of the area removed by holes, PETG at 1.27 g/cm³, 90% effective density. At this thickness the walls and top/bottom layers are solid anyway, so 80% and 100% infill give almost the same weight.

| Thickness | Per plate | 2 plates |
|---|---|---|
| 3 mm | about 90 g | about 180 g |
| 4 mm | about 120 g | about 240 g |
| 5 mm | about 150 g | about 300 g |

(A 150 mm plate would be about 22% lighter.)

## Revised robot total

| | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| 2 plates | 120–200 g | **180–300 g** |
| Everything else | 530–650 g | 530–650 g |
| **Total** | 650–850 g | **about 710–950 g** |

**The motor sizing doesn't change.** I had already sized the motors for 1.0 kg, and even 5 mm plates keep the robot under that. Everything from the last answer still holds:
- **Motors:** 6 V geared motors at about 200 RPM, with a stall torque of at least 1.0–1.5 kg·cm. They draw about 0.2–0.4 A each while driving, and should stall at 1.5 A or less.
- **System:** a 2S 18650 battery (7.4 V) and a BMS rated for 8 A or more. Expect about 1.2–1.5 A in normal driving and 5–6 A peak.
- **Drivers:** 2 dual drivers, so each motor gets its own channel.

One design note: 80–100% infill isn't needed for a 3–4 mm plate. About 40% infill with 3–4 walls around the edges and around each hole is nearly as stiff, saves about 20–30% of the plate weight, and prints faster. It's only worth changing if you reprint anyway.
